extracted.intended_audience: artists, art students, art historians, and educated readers of art criticism interested in iconography and moral representation
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating personification and symbolism in art
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for how virtues, vices, and abstract ideas should be symbolized or personified in painting and sculpture; includes how to choose symbols, avoid common errors, and fit iconography to religious or social context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolism vs Personification
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbolism: setting forth of a great truth by an imperfect and inferior sign (e.g., the phoenix for hope of the resurrection). Personification: bestowing a human or living form upon an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor symbolism for solemn, serious truths and religious moods—men who use symbolism forcibly are almost always true believers in what they symbolize. Personification is generally less noble, often a recreation of fancy, and apt to disturb belief in the reality of the thing personified; use personification cautiously and only when rooted in genuine spiritual/intellectual conviction. Examples: Christ's teaching uses symbolism almost exclusively; Dante's imagery uses powerful personification but remains spiritual because of his faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confusing duties with virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not enumerate particular duties, works, or offices of charity as if they were separate virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware morbid accuracy of classification that lists many charitable acts as distinct virtues (e.g., listing multiple works of mercy as separate virtues). Keep the distinction between a moral virtue (habit of character) and discrete acts or duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification requires spiritual/intellectual foundation
rubrics_metrics.description: Personification is noble when conceived by masters whose fancy does not overthrow the foundations of faith; early earnest masters produced personifications that are spiritual and vital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the conceiver's faith/intellect is weak or merely fanciful, personification becomes superficial. Compare noble personifications (Dante's burning Charity) with more prosaic or domestic renderings (Reynolds's nurse Charity) to judge depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit the system of virtues to the life/context depicted
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice and arrangement of virtues and their personifications must reflect the religion, social role, or way of life the artist intends to illustrate (e.g., monkish life vs general mankind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select virtues appropriate to the scene: Giotto at Assisi emphasizes Franciscan virtues (Chastity, Obedience, Poverty) with attendant virtues appropriate to monastic life; in civic or general settings, prefer the theological and cardinal virtues. Do not mechanically transplant one system to another context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use opposing vices to clarify virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Personified vices placed opposite virtues often reveal the precise idea of the virtue intended by the artist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The contraposition helps refine meaning: e.g., Prudence opposed by Folly indicates 'Heavenly Wisdom' rather than mere guidance. Use deliberate oppositions to communicate nuances of the intended virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness and specificity of visual attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete physical attributes (poses, objects, dress, tools) should be chosen to signal the precise character of the virtue or vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose symbols that support the intended moral idea (e.g., Folly: half-naked man eating an apple and brandishing a club -> sensuality and violence; Despair: dagger in throat and torn hair; Faith: cross and creed-scroll; Temperance: bridle on lips and sword). Avoid vague or domesticated substitutes that weaken the idea (e.g., substituting a plate for showered gold or turning a tragic Despair into a coiffed figure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth and moral/profound truth in depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtues should be depicted with spiritual or philosophical profundity, not merely formal labels or decorative gestures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More profound systems (Dante, Spenser) require greater attention and a 'holier heart' to appreciate; strive for depiction that expresses inner reality (e.g., Dante's Paradise) rather than surface allegory. Anti-pattern: thin, conventional, or sentimental renderings that strip away spiritual weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity when iconography is ambiguous—use inscriptions or clearer signs
rubrics_metrics.description: When a sculptural or pictorial figure is not self-explanatory, inscriptions or explicit attributes may be necessary to convey meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: some capitals required inscriptions to identify 'Discordia' because the figure alone was unclear. Where ambiguity would confuse viewers, add textual labels or stronger, conventional attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance should be shown as moderation of all passions (not mere abstinence)
rubrics_metrics.description: True Temperance (Greek sôphrosynê) is the moderator of all passions and involves prudence; not merely the opposite of gluttony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict Temperance as controlling and regulating desires (e.g., bridle upon lips, binding sword to scabbard), not just abstaining from food/drink. Anti-pattern: depicting Temperance only as a water-pitcher or cup (mere abstinence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence should emphasize forethought or anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prudence's distinctive character is forethought (not merely cautiousness or book-learning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iconography should show vigilance and ability to consider many things (Giotto's Janus-headed Prudence with convex mirror and compasses). Avoid static images that suggest only calculation; include symbols of foresight and comprehensive view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charity should express love and spiritual fervor, not mere munificence
rubrics_metrics.description: Charity is more than generosity; in noble iconography it is love inflamed, often shown by flames or a cross of fire, not only by hands distributing alms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict Charity with signs of enlivening love (glory, flame, reception of treasure from Christ) rather than purely material abundance. Anti-pattern: a domestic mother-with-children motif that reduces Charity to sentimental benevolence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as active, sovereign weighing
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice should be shown as an active ruler with instruments of judgment (crown, sword) and the capacity to weigh causes herself (e.g., holding scales in each hand).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer images that show Justice making decisions, not passive balance: Giotto's enthroned Justice holding a scale in each hand suggests her immediate agency. Include emblems that show both punishment and reward to express judicial scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fortitude should transcend mere courage to imply sustained strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Fortitude is not simply manly courage; proper depictions express enduring strength and resistance (e.g., clothed with lion's skin, immovable shield).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vulgar or anecdotal personifications that reduce Fortitude to a brute act (e.g., a bearded man tearing a lion's jaw) when the concept intended is higher. Use iconography (tower-like shield, sword poised behind shield) that communicates guarded, steadfast strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hope as a distinctively Christian and testing virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Hope is the clearly Christian virtue that tests whether one is truly Christian—longing and expectation of heaven are its marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict Hope with devotional, upward-looking attitude, gestures of prayer, winged ascent, or a hand extended from heaven; show longing and expectation rather than passive optimism. Because it 'tests' Christianity, its depiction should be spiritually expressive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patience as a principal and beneficent Christian virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Patience should be represented as steadfast, calm, and beneficent—often a principal virtue in Christian systems (sometimes masculine), with the capacity to heal or minister.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual attributes: composed posture, hand on breast, hooded modesty; literary parallels: described as Physician in Spenser's House of Holiness. Avoid conflating Patience with mere passivity or weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Despair as the proper opposite of Hope—show extreme anguish
rubrics_metrics.description: Despair must be depicted with intense self-destruction and physical anguish (e.g., dagger in throat, tearing hair), not trivialized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray destructive, hopeless gestures; anti-pattern: Renaissance copies that remove expression or sanitize the anguish into mere coiffed ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obedience's depiction varies by system—emphasize humility and submission where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Obedience is a central virtue in monkish systems; iconography should show meek submission, yoking, or ritual acts of subordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: folded arms, a small dog begging as a symbol, an angel passing a yoke over a monk's head. In non-monastic contexts, avoid overstating Obedience where it is less central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infidelity as bondage and obstruction of light
rubrics_metrics.description: Infidelity should be shown as bound to images or idols and deprived of light or truth (e.g., helmeted, heavy drapery, bound by cord to an image).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey spiritual blindness and the weight of false belief; depict the image/idol as a physical burden. Avoid bland or neutral portraits that fail to indicate spiritual error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural/regional selection of virtues matters (industry/honesty emphasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different cultures or regions emphasize different virtues (e.g., Venetian list includes honesty and alacrity; Northern art and morality prize industry and honesty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing an iconographic program, include virtues that reflect local civic or moral priorities. The absence of industry/honesty in some Italian lists but presence in Northern lists is not an oversight but cultural variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of composition and placement to support narrative read
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrangement, order, and positioning of personified figures (e.g., on capitals, in chariot procession) contributes to meaning and should be considered in design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count sides, order from vantage point, and arrange attendant virtues and vices to support the central theological narrative (e.g., the chariot of the Deity attended by theological and cardinal virtues). Consider visibility and which faces of a multi-sided element will be seen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sentimentalization and vulgarization of high allegory
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reduce profound allegory and spiritual personifications to commonplace or sentimental images merely because they are more 'handsome' or decorative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns include Renaissance or later copies that 'smooth' expressive severity into pleasant domestic scenes (e.g., soft-faced children replacing energetic medieval children; Despair turned into a coiffed figure). Preserve the original moral intensity where intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iconographic detail should be historically and materially attentive
rubrics_metrics.description: Material and sculptural details (leaf arrangement, number and placement of figures, tools, crowns, compasses) matter for legibility and historical fidelity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to classical conventions (e.g., octagonal capitals with sixteen leaves and grouped figures), and use period-appropriate attributes to strengthen authenticity. Small changes for 'decoration' often injure the conceptual clarity of the original.
